When something is described as highbrow, it means it is intellectual, serious, and culturally sophisticated — the kind of thing associated with deep thinking, high education, and refined taste. It describes ideas, art, entertainment, or people that operate at a level that requires significant knowledge, intelligence, or cultural background to fully appreciate.

Think of it this way: highbrow things don't make life easy for you. They challenge you, demand your full attention, and expect you to bring some knowledge or education to the table.
What Kinds of Things Are Called "Highbrow"?

The word is used very broadly across culture and the arts:

  • Literature: A dense philosophical novel by Dostoevsky is highbrow. A gossip magazine is not.
  • Music: A classical symphony performed at a concert hall is highbrow. A catchy pop song on the radio is not.
  • Film: A slow, subtitled foreign film exploring the meaning of human existence is highbrow. A loud action blockbuster is not.
  • Conversation: Discussing the ethics of artificial intelligence or debating political philosophy is highbrow. Chatting about last night's football game is not.
  • Humour: A joke that depends on knowing Latin or referencing ancient Greek myths is highbrow humour.

The common thread in all these examples is intellectual seriousness and sophistication.

When you call a person highbrow, you mean they are deeply intellectual and tend to prefer serious, complex, or elite cultural experiences over popular ones. A highbrow person might spend their weekends reading academic essays, attending the opera, and discussing philosophy — and might have little interest in (or may even quietly look down on) simple, mass-market entertainment.

This is an important point: when used to describe people, "highbrow" often carries a slight edge of criticism. It can suggest that the person is a little snobby or elitist — that they consider themselves intellectually superior and look down on ordinary people's tastes.

So the word can be used in two slightly different ways:

  1. Neutral or admiring: "She has very highbrow taste in literature." (She reads serious, intellectual books — stated as a simple fact or even a compliment.)
  2. Mildly critical: "He's so highbrow — he refused to watch anything that isn't a foreign art film." (He's being a snob about it.)

The context and tone of the speaker's voice (or writing) usually make it clear which meaning is intended.

To truly understand "highbrow," it helps to know its opposite: lowbrow.

  • Lowbrow describes things (or people) that are simple, unsophisticated, and aimed at popular mass audiences — slapstick comedy, reality TV, fast food culture, trashy novels. There is no intellectual demand placed on you. You just consume and enjoy.
  • Highbrow is at the other end of the scale — demanding, intellectual, and often associated with elite or academic culture.
  • Right in the middle sits middlebrow — things that are reasonably intelligent and culturally respectable, but still accessible and enjoyable to a wide audience. A well-made historical drama on television, for example, might be described as middlebrow.

These three words together paint a full picture of the cultural spectrum.

Not necessarily, and this is a subtle but important point. Calling something highbrow is a description of its intellectual level and cultural style — it is not automatically a judgment of quality. Something can be highbrow and brilliant, but something can also be highbrow and boring, pretentious, or unnecessarily difficult. Equally, something lowbrow can be genuinely joyful, creative, and deeply entertaining.

The word tells you what kind of thing it is, not whether it is good or bad.

• "The documentary was a little too highbrow for me — I couldn't follow all the philosophical references."
  • "She moved in highbrow intellectual circles, attending lectures and literary salons."
  • "The magazine tried to strike a balance between highbrow analysis and stories that everyday readers could enjoy."
  • "His humour was so highbrow that half the audience didn't get the jokes."
  • "The play was considered highbrow entertainment — the kind of thing critics loved but general audiences avoided."
Highbrow means intellectually sophisticated, serious, and associated with elite culture and education — and when used about people, it can suggest they are a bit of a snob about it.
